lead: Very deep CNNs hit two problems: many kernel sizes may matter, and gradients vanish. Inception runs 1×1, 3×3, 5×5 convolutions and pooling in parallel, then concatenates the results, so one block sees small and large patterns. ResNet adds a shortcut that carries the input around a block: y = F(x) + x. The shortcut gives gradients a short path, so 50 to 152 layers train. These blocks power ImageNet classifiers and pretrained backbones used in transfer learning.
prereq: You need: 3.3, 3.4, and the vanishing-gradient section in Unit 2.

blocks.text: A plain CNN can be made deeper by stacking more 3×3 layers. Past a point, training error rises even on the training set. This is the degradation problem, not overfitting. The extra layers are hard to optimize: an identity mapping should be easy, yet many layers fail to learn it.

ResNet makes identity easy. A residual block computes a convolution path F(x) and adds the input x. If F is near zero, the block passes x unchanged. Gradients also flow through the addition, a short path back. This is separate from the vanishing-gradient fixes in Unit 2; it gives depth a highway.

blocks.where: x is the block input feature map; F(x) is the output of the convolution path; y is the block output after the addition and ReLU.

blocks.text: The bottleneck block uses 1×1 conv to reduce channels, 3×3 conv to work at low channel count, and 1×1 conv to expand back. ResNet-50, ResNet-101 and ResNet-152 stack these blocks. A basic block uses two 3×3 convs instead.

items: An identity shortcut works when F(x) and x have the same height, width and channels.
If channels change or stride is greater than 1, use a 1×1 projection W_s with matching stride: y = F(x) + W_s x.

blocks.text: Inception asks which kernel size is right. A 1×1, 3×3 and 5×5 kernel see different scales. Instead of choosing, run all in parallel. An input feature map of size H×W×C goes to four branches: a 1×1 conv; a 1×1 conv then a 3×3 conv; a 1×1 conv then a 5×5 conv; and a 3×3 max pool then a 1×1 conv.

Each branch outputs H×W×c_i, where c_i is that branch's channel count. Concatenate along the channel axis to get H×W×(c1+c3+c5+cp). The 1×1 convs before the 3×3 and 5×5 branches are bottlenecks: they cut C to a small number, so a 5×5 conv does not cost C×25×C_out.

blocks.where: Y1, Y3, Y5 and Yp are the branch outputs with the same H and W; concat joins them along the channel axis.

blocks.text: Padding keeps H and W unchanged in every branch. The pooling branch also uses padding. Inception concatenates branch outputs; it never adds them. GoogLeNet is Inception v1. Later versions factorize large kernels, but the parallel idea stays.

DenseNet connects each layer to every later layer inside a dense block. Layer l receives the concatenation of all earlier feature maps in that block. With L layers there are L(L+1)/2 direct connections. Each layer adds only a few new channels, called the growth rate k; common values are 12 to 32. Features are reused, so parameters can be smaller.

A transition layer after each dense block reduces channels and spatial size. This keeps the concatenated tensor from growing too fast. The main exam idea is the connection pattern, not the full DenseNet schedule.

Compare the tensor operation. Inception concatenates parallel branches inside one block. ResNet adds a shortcut across a block. DenseNet concatenates across depth. All three improve gradient flow and feature mixing, but add and concatenate are not interchangeable.

figure.caption: The bottleneck squeezes 64 channels to 16, works at 3 × 3, and expands back to 64, costing 1040 + 2320 + 1088 = 4448 parameters. Because the output is again 56 × 56 × 64, the shortcut can add the input back unchanged.

examples.question: A ResNet bottleneck receives a 56×56×64 feature map. A 1×1 conv makes 16 channels, a 3×3 conv with 16 filters and pad 1 keeps the size, and a 1×1 conv makes 64 channels. An identity shortcut skips the three convs. Find the output shape and the total parameters of the three conv layers, counting weights and biases.
steps: Input size is H=56, W=56, C=64. Conv1 is 1×1 with 16 filters: output is 56×56×16. Its parameters are 1×1×64×16 weights plus 16 biases = 1024 + 16 = 1040.
Conv2 is 3×3 with 16 input channels, 16 filters, stride 1 and pad 1. Output is 56×56×16. Parameters are 3×3×16×16 weights plus 16 biases = 2304 + 16 = 2320.
Conv3 is 1×1 with 16 input channels and 64 filters. Output is 56×56×64. Parameters are 1×1×16×64 weights plus 64 biases = 1024 + 64 = 1088.
The identity shortcut needs the same shape as the conv path output. Both are 56×56×64, so the addition is valid. Total parameters = 1040 + 2320 + 1088 = 4448.
examples.answer: The output is 56×56×64, and the three conv layers have 4448 parameters in total.

traps: A shortcut adds tensors; Inception concatenates branch outputs along channels. Writing that Inception adds its branches loses marks.
Addition needs identical shapes. When channels change or stride is 2, use a 1×1 projection shortcut with matching stride; a plain identity shortcut will not broadcast.
In a 1×1 conv from C_in to C_out, parameters are C_in×C_out + C_out, not H×W×C_in×C_out. Bias is one per output channel.
The degradation problem is higher training error in a deeper plain network, not overfitting. ResNet fixes optimization, not just test-set variance.
Inception's 3×3 and 5×5 branches use padding to keep H and W equal; otherwise concatenation along channels fails.

quiz.q: What operation does an Inception module use to combine its parallel branches?
quiz.a: It concatenates the branch outputs along the channel axis, producing one feature map with the sum of the branch channel counts.

quiz.q: Why does an identity shortcut help train a very deep ResNet?
quiz.a: The shortcut gives gradients a short path back to earlier layers. The conv path only has to learn a residual F(x), and if F is near zero the block passes x unchanged.

quiz.q: A 1×1 conv takes 128 input channels and produces 32 output channels. How many parameters does it have, including bias?
An Inception block receives 28×28×192 input. Its four branches output 64, 128, 32 and 32 channels, all at 28×28. What is the output shape?
quiz.a: Spatial size stays 28×28. Channels add: 64 + 128 + 32 + 32 = 256. Output is 28×28×256.

quiz.q: Why can an Inception block concatenate branches with different channel counts, while a ResNet shortcut normally cannot add tensors with different channel counts?
quiz.a: Concatenation stacks feature maps along a new channel axis, so unequal channel counts are fine. Addition combines values position by position, so both tensors must have the same height, width and channels.

quiz.q: State the difference between the degradation problem and overfitting.
quiz.a: Degradation means a deeper plain network has higher training error than a shallower one. Overfitting means training error is low but test error is high. ResNet targets degradation by making identity mappings easy to learn.

quiz.q: A residual block has input 56×56×64 and the conv path output is 28×28×128. What shortcut is needed?
quiz.a: A plain identity fails because both spatial size and channels differ. Use a 1×1 conv projection with stride 2 to map 56×56×64 to 28×28×128, then add it to the conv path output.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern backbones mix these ideas: EfficientNet uses compound scaling, ConvNeXt borrows large kernels, and Transformers use residual connections. Search 'ResNet bottleneck', 'Inception module' and 'DenseNet growth rate' to see implementations. Torchvision and TensorFlow model zoos ship pretrained versions for transfer learning.
